Posted August 7, 2002
Special report by Richard Cowan

This weekend I returned from a three-week trip to The Netherlands, which I spent in the beautiful city of Haarlem.

Haarlem, which is just fifteen minutes by train ($5 round trip) from Amsterdam's Centraal Station, really is one of the loveliest places I have ever been, but that is not the reason that I was there.
See

As regular readers might guess, the immediate cause of my being in Haarlem was Nol van Schaik, owner of the

As I wrote in 2000, the great thing about Haarlem -- from a political perspective -- is that it is a much more " typical " Dutch city than Amsterdam. Amsterdam has a population of roughly 700,000, but has ten times that many visitors. Haarlem, has a population of 150,000, and few visitors. Moreover, in Amsterdam some of the bigger shops are allowed to sell alcohol, but that is not allowed in the rest of Holland. Consequently, if someone from another country -- or another planet like DEAland wants to get an idea about how the coffeeshop system works, Haarlem might be a better example than Amsterdam for most.

And that is where Nol van Schaik comes in. Nol is far more politically sophisticated than most shop owners. He is very articulate speaks English very well, and as a former competitive bodybuilder, he is certainly not bashful.

Since then, Nol has also the co-founded

Unfortunately, things are not going so well in the UK right now, because the Blair government seems intent on ignoring the Dutch experience in general, and the rights of the people from the Dutch Experience coffee shop, in particular.
See

But in Haarlem things are going very well indeed. By standing up for his rights, Nol has helped the Haarlem police and city government craft realistic regulations for cannabis cafes.
See

As a part of my professional duties, I spent quite a bit of time in Nol's shops. (Work, work, work!)

Actually, it was very interesting, and one of them is even air-conditioned. (An air-conditioned coffee shop is a pretty good idea of heaven for this Texan.)

Although I have been in Holland many times, and have smoked at cannabis friendly places in Vancouver, and elsewhere, there is always a period of adjustment as I get used to the Dutch experience of freedom.

First, it seems quite remarkable how unremarkable the coffee shops are in The Netherlands.

Because Nol has a reputation for quality cannabis, there was always a steady stream of customers -- who did not fit any stereotype, and most of them bought their cannabis for take-out. (Prices range from around US$4 per gram up to $12 for the best. And the $4 stuff is very good.)

I watched them for a while.

A plainly-dressed middle-aged woman, who looked like a small town housewife, was followed by a young man who looked like he had just left his bank job. While the average customers appeared to be twenty-something, many were older. One nicely dressed lady, walking with a limp, appeared to be a medical user.

(Nol gives 50% discounts to patients with a doctor's letter, as a part of the MediWiet program founded by Wernerd Bruining of Positronic fame. That was really the world's first medical cannabis program.)
See

In short, cannabis is used by a cross section of Dutch society, which one will not see in the tourist areas of Amsterdam.

In fact, one of the funniest comments by a prohibitionist opposed to cannabis cafes came from Alistair Ramsay, the director of Scotland Against Drugs, who said: " The Dutch experience does not give the answers that so many of those who propose the adoption of cannabis cafes in Scotland believe will.

" In Holland, the Dutch people are very concerned that the majority of people using the cannabis cafes are not Dutch. What these have become are magnets for people to come into the country to smoke cannabis. "

Obviously, Mr Ramsey must spend too much time in Amsterdam's Red Light district, as seems to be the case with visiting prohibitionists.

In Haarlem, I was usually the only foreigner in the shops, and the natives seemed to be very friendly! Of course, it is comical to think that the Dutch would object to foreigners spending money, and it seems even more unlike the Scots to tell people to take their money elsewhere!

But Mr. Ramsey is precisely wrong when he says that " The Dutch experience does not give the answers "

On the contrary, the Dutch experience does give the answers to those who wonder what happens when cannabis is effectively legalized.

Unfortunately, the prohibitionist propaganda machine has lied so much about the Dutch experience for so long that Mr. Ramsey's comical misperceptions are the least of it.
See

So that is where the book comes in.

Over the next few months I am going to be writing a book to be called surprise, surprise -- The Dutch Experience, which will be a short history of the coffee shop movement and its impact on the Dutch cannabis policies,

The book will not pretend to be a complete history of the coffee shops. That will have to wait until later. The objective will be to describe the various aspects of the Dutch experience in getting and enjoying freedom. It will also contrast what happened in The Netherlands with the DEAland experience, and the UK experience, etc.

The importance of the Dutch experience is that it demonstrates that " freedom works " -- as the uncomprehending G.H.W. Bush used to say.

The key point is not that Dutch cannabis use rates are generally lower than in many prohibitionist countries. That is not the proper measure of the success of cannabis policies. What is really important is that hard drug use in The Netherlands is much lower than in prohibitionist countries, and they have avoided the hideous cost of arresting large numbers of their citizens.
See
The Theory and Practice of Chaos Analysis By Richard Cowan

I am already enjoying pulling together my notes for the book, and because I have written so much on the subject over the last few years, it will be relatively easy and fast to write.

Nonetheless, for the next four months I am going to have to restrict MarijuanaNews.com to two weekly updates.

The good news is that I will also post excerpts from the book during this time, to give you a taste for well The Dutch Experience.

And the even better news is that -- if all goes according to plan I will be moving to Haarlem in the fall, and I hope that all of you will come for a visit, then Alistair Ramsey can go to Willie Wortel's and talk about the foreigners annoying the natives.
